title: From decision to settlement: how Korean immigrant parents raising a child with disabilities respond to disabling socio-educational environments
authors: Yoon H. Lee, Jisun Lee, Jinwoo Lee
abstract: This phenomenological study examines the lived experiences of six Korean mothers who immigrated to the United States to seek more inclusive educational opportunities and post-school supports for their children with disabilities. Grounded in disability studies, the analysis traces parents’ narratives across three stages: the decision to migrate, early settlement, and long-term adjustment. Findings reveal that migration was driven by structural barriers in Korea, concerns for children’s adulthood, and parents’ belief that more supportive systems existed abroad. After immigrating, parents became proactive advocates and navigated linguistic, cultural, and bureaucratic barriers while developing expertise within U.S. service systems. Over time, parents described greater satisfaction with educational and disability services while continuing to experience emotional strain, and redefined their quality of life, independence, and belonging. This study highlights how immigration becomes a prolonged journey where families emerge as active agents in resisting disabling environments and rebuilding possibilities for their children’s futures.

title: Disability type matters: structural discrimination in employment access and retention in Turkey
abstract: Despite legal frameworks, quota obligations, employment incentives and active labour market programmes, the par­ticipation of people with disabilities in Turkey’s labour market remains limited. Turkey is a salient case because a developing-country labour market coexists with an extensive formal policy framework whose inclusive effects are constrained by weak enforcement, fragmented institutional coordination and persistent social prejudice. Based on semi-structured interviews with employees with disabilities, employers, İŞKUR officials, NGO representatives and parents of disabled individuals, this study examines structural barriers to employment access and retention. The findings show that discrimination varies by disability type. People with visible, severe, intellectual or psychosocial disabilities face stronger exclusion during recruitment, while those with invisible or milder disabilities are often preferred. Concerns about safety, productivity and workplace adaptation confine many disabled workers to low-skilled and low-visibility jobs. Policy gaps further undermine inclusion. The study argues for a contextual and interactional understanding of disability employment.

title: Ambiguities on disabled bodies in artworks: a Critical Iconology perspective
abstract: This research situates itself at the intersection of disability studies and visual studies, employing a methodology informed by Critical Iconology as developed by Aby Warburg to analyze the representation of the disabled body in artworks in the twentieth century. It critiques and extends the discourse around the cultural perception of disability, by examining visual representations of impairment across diverse artworks between1920–1999. The study collects and maps images of the disabled body from different periods, examining the meanings of signs and patterns of impairment by adopting the critical theoretical frame of the social model of disability and ableism. Critical Iconology provides the tools to understand what the images say through cultural and social political circumstances. This research seeks to dismantle stereotypes and advance a nuanced understanding of the disabled body as depicted in visual arts.

title: Accessibility or misbehaviour: ableism in theatres
abstract: Recent public debates about actors challenging audience members’ smartphone use during live theatre performances have foregrounded etiquette, distraction and theatrical immersion while overlooking smartphones’ role in enabling disabled people’s cultural participation. This article examines the tensions between normative expectations of audience behaviour and the use of smartphones as interfaces for accessibility technologies. Drawing on scholarship on ableism, psycho-emotional disablism and disability disclosure, it argues that framing smartphone use as inherently inappropriate reproduces exclusionary assumptions about legitimate participation. Disabled audience members risk having their access needs misrecognised, experiencing scrutiny and feeling compelled to disclose personal information to justify their behaviour. Such pressures can undermine belonging and discourage cultural participation. The article argues for an ethics of anticipatory access, in which theatres and cultural organisations develop policies that recognise diverse modes of participation without requiring disabled people to explain or defend their needs. It positions accessibility as a shared institutional responsibility rather than an individual accommodation.

title: Leading the pack: assistance dog team instruction from a universal design perspective
abstract: This article examines how disabled assistance dog professionals adapt traditional work practice norms to meet their needs and those of clients and assistance dogs. Based on nine interviews and 16 survey responses collected from disabled assistance dog professionals and their clients across Europe, this article identifies adaptations involving communication, session planning and structure, technology use, and, at times, the involvement of the professional’s assistance dog as their co-worker. Rather than solely compensating for disability, professionals frequently innovate more traditional practices that benefit the assistance dog team, offering potential new ways to approach instruction for the broader assistance dog sector to consider. The article speaks to a significant gap in literature concerning the work of assistance dog professionals with disabilities, and provides data to support a more accessible and inclusive assistance dog sector through universal design.

title: Families as subjects of need and knowledge: epistemic misrecognition in disability welfare policy in Norway
abstract: This article explores how Norwegian welfare policies aiming to ‘recognize families as resources’ align with the lived experiences of families caring for children with multiple disabilities. Drawing on qualitative data, the article examines parents’ experiences through a lens of professional family partnership and theories of epistemic injustice and social recognition. The article develops the notion of ‘epistemic misrecognition’ to describe three dimensions of feeling unacknowledged in these family accounts: families feel unheard in their testimony (testimonial misrecognition); they feel dismissed as relevant participants in inquiry (participatory misrecognition); and especially mothers experience misrecognition of their care-based expertise (misrecognition of experiential knowledge). These findings underscore both the importance of valuing families’ expertise in policy and practice and the barriers to doing so. While Norwegian next-of-kin policies recognise families as subjects of need, they are less able to acknowledge families as subjects of knowledge and fall short in granting families full epistemic standing.

title: Having choices and being supported: a co-research project about independence and Down syndrome
authors: Ashley Scott, Staci Christensen, Augusta Edouard, Benjamin Golden
abstract: Independence can look different for each person. People with Down syndrome are living longer, and many get support from professionals to grow their independence. We wanted to understand how health professionals support independence for people with Down syndrome. We used co-research method where team members with Down syndrome collaborate on all stages of the research process. Co-researchers interviewed 8 health professionals and 2 with Down syndrome about independence. We asked about communication, daily life skills, health, employment, and independent living. Using an inclusive process, we analyzed our data by coding transcripts, finding big ideas and patterns, then came up with themes. We found that health professionals mostly support independence for health, communication, and life skills. They want adults with Down syndrome to be independent, make choices, and get help from others when needed.
